stories.headline: Small open-weight models are becoming genuinely useful on a student laptop
stories.dek: An illustrative look at why compact models that run locally change what students can prototype without cloud credits.
body: This is a sample story used to demonstrate the AI//CAMPUS reading experience. It does not report a specific announcement.

Compact language models with a few billion parameters can now be run on consumer hardware using quantisation and runtimes such as llama.cpp or Ollama. For students, that shifts experimentation from “who has API credits” to “who has a laptop”.

Local models are slower and less capable than the largest hosted systems, and their quality varies widely by task. The practical skill is learning to evaluate a model on your own problem rather than trusting a leaderboard.
When the live feed is connected, this space will carry the verified summary, the original source link, and the publication date from the source itself.

impact.whyItMatters: You can prototype AI features offline, keep data private, and learn how models actually behave under constraints.
impact.buildIdea: A private study assistant that answers questions from your own lecture notes without sending them to a server.

stories.headline: Browser-using agents: what they can do today, and where they still fail
stories.dek: A sample explainer on agents that click, type and navigate, and why reliability is the open problem.
body: This is a sample story used to demonstrate the interface.
Agent systems combine a language model with tools: a browser, a code runner, a file system. The model plans a step, calls a tool, reads the result and decides what to do next.
The hard part is not a single step but a long chain of them. Small error rates compound, so evaluation on realistic multi-step tasks matters more than impressive demos.

impact.whyItMatters: Agents are becoming a common interface to software. Understanding their failure modes is a durable engineering skill.
impact.buildIdea: An agent that fills a timetable from a course page, with a log of every action it took so you can audit it.

stories.headline: Why open Indian-language speech data matters for the next wave of apps
stories.dek: A sample piece on how open datasets lower the barrier for students building voice tools in regional languages.
body: This is a sample story used to demonstrate the interface.
Speech recognition quality depends heavily on training data. Many Indian languages have historically had little open, well-labelled audio, which limits what independent developers can build.
Open datasets and models from Indian research groups let students fine-tune and evaluate systems for languages and accents that global products often under-serve.

impact.whyItMatters: There is real, local demand for tools that work in Hindi, Garhwali, Kumaoni and other languages around Dehradun.
impact.buildIdea: A voice note transcriber for a local language, with a small test set recorded by classmates (with consent).

stories.headline: How to read a model card before you trust a model
stories.dek: A sample guide to the documentation that tells you what a model was trained for, and what it was not.
body: This is a sample story used to demonstrate the interface.
Model cards describe intended use, training data at a high level, evaluation results and known limitations. They are the first place to check before using a model in a project.
Look for what was measured, on which data, and what the authors say the model should not be used for.

impact.whyItMatters: Choosing the wrong model is the most common reason student AI projects disappoint.
impact.buildIdea: A one-page comparison of three models for your project, written from their cards and your own tests.

stories.headline: Agent frameworks are converging on the same few ideas
stories.dek: A sample overview of the shared building blocks behind popular agent libraries.
body: This is a sample story used to demonstrate the interface.
Most agent frameworks provide the same primitives: a loop, tool definitions, memory, and some way to trace what happened. Learning the primitives transfers between libraries.

impact.whyItMatters: Frameworks change quickly. Concepts last longer than any one library.
impact.buildIdea: Implement a minimal agent loop from scratch in under 150 lines before adopting a framework.

stories.headline: What AI governance debates mean for people still in university
stories.dek: A sample explainer on why transparency, data rights and accountability are becoming engineering requirements.
body: This is a sample story used to demonstrate the interface.
Rules about AI increasingly ask builders to document data sources, test for harmful outputs and explain decisions. These are engineering tasks, not just legal ones.

impact.whyItMatters: Law, management and engineering students will all meet AI governance questions in their first jobs.
impact.buildIdea: Write a short risk assessment for a classmate’s AI project and agree on mitigations together.

stories.headline: Multimodal models read diagrams now. Use them to check, not to copy
stories.dek: A sample note on models that understand images and text together, and how to use them responsibly for study.
body: This is a sample story used to demonstrate the interface.
Models that accept images can explain a circuit diagram or a chart. They also make confident mistakes, so treat their output as a hypothesis to verify.

impact.whyItMatters: Used well, they are a patient tutor. Used carelessly, they undermine your own understanding.
impact.buildIdea: A flashcard generator that turns photographed lecture slides into questions, then cites the slide each came from.

stories.headline: A three-pass method for reading an arXiv paper in under an hour
stories.dek: A sample guide to skimming, understanding and critiquing research without getting lost.
body: This is a sample story used to demonstrate the interface.
Pass one: title, abstract, figures and conclusion. Pass two: method and experiments. Pass three: what would you test to break the claim?

impact.whyItMatters: Reading papers well is the fastest way to stay ahead of headlines that oversell results.
impact.buildIdea: Reproduce one figure from a small paper and write up what matched and what did not.

stories.headline: Shipped projects tell a clearer story than a stack of certificates
stories.dek: A sample career note on documenting AI work so others can evaluate it.
body: This is a sample story used to demonstrate the interface. It is general guidance, not a prediction about hiring.
A small, working, well-documented project shows judgement: what you chose, what you measured, and what you would do next.

impact.whyItMatters: Evidence of real work is easier for anyone to assess than a list of courses.
impact.buildIdea: Pick your best class project and add an evaluation section and a two-minute demo.

stories.headline: Try retrieval before fine-tuning: a practical rule for student projects
stories.dek: A sample explainer on when to add your documents to a prompt and when to train a model.
body: This is a sample story used to demonstrate the interface.
Retrieval-augmented generation fetches relevant passages and gives them to the model at answer time. It is cheaper and easier to update than fine-tuning, and usually the right first step.

impact.whyItMatters: Most “chat with your documents” projects need retrieval, not training.
impact.buildIdea: A Q&A tool over your department’s public syllabus PDFs, with citations for every answer.

briefing.title: Edition 03 · Smaller models, bigger reach
transcript: Welcome to the AI//CAMPUS sixty-second briefing. This is a sample transcript used to preview the format.
This week’s sample edition looks at compact open models you can run on a laptop, and why that changes how students prototype.
We also cover browser-using agents and where they still fail, why open Indian-language speech data matters, and how to read a model card before trusting a model.
Your one thing to try: write thirty real examples from your project and test two models against them.
